bridges.claim: At least one coherent non-theistic account of moral truth defeats the claimed necessity of God.
Impersonal goodness, rational agency, and Buddhist compassion offer distinct candidate foundations.
Theistic and non-theistic systems alike reach an ultimate good; history and causal explanation do not establish exclusive grounding.
Christian narrative may powerfully motivate compassion without deductively excluding alternative narratives.
The scope of moral obligation and disagreements between first principles require distinctions, not a simple subjective/objective binary.

routes.speaker: Glen Scrivener
routes.position: Humanistic goodness finds its true foundation in Christ

bridges.claim: The true foundation of humanistic equality, rights, and care for the weak is Jesus Christ, not mere atheist or theist behavior.
Human equality is not empirically self-evident; its Christian genealogy points to its metaphysical foundation.
Incarnation, cross, and eternal personal love supply a fitting ultimate good and privilege the vulnerable.
Evolutionary cooperation and in-group reciprocity do not supply the Christian ethic of enemy-love and protecting the weak.
Experienced obligations and outrage resist a merely private morality.
Jesus supplies a narrative framework for interpreting nonideal Old Testament rules.
